config.materials:
Balloon
Plastic straw
4 bottle caps (wheels)
Skewers or toothpicks (axles)
Cardboard or lightweight plastic sheet
Tape
Scissors
config.learn: Air pushes the car forward when it escapes the balloon (Newton's Third Law). The experiment demonstrates action-reaction forces and friction effects.

steps: Cut the cardboard to a rectangle (around 15 x 10 cm) to form the car base.
Push skewers through the cardboard horizontally to make axles.
Attach bottle caps to the ends of skewers as wheels. Secure with tape if needed.
Tape a straw along the top of the cardboard so that the balloon's opening points backward.
Inflate the balloon, pinch it closed, and place it in the straw.
Release the balloon and watch your car move forward.
Try different balloon sizes or car weights to see which moves fastest.

config.materials:
Rubber bands (various sizes)
Popsicle sticks (2–3)
Tape
Small lightweight object (paper ball, pom-pom)
config.learn: Elastic potential energy stored in the rubber band converts to kinetic energy. You can observe how energy transfer and tension affect motion.

steps: Stack two popsicle sticks together and secure with tape to make a launcher base.
Stretch a rubber band between the sticks so it can hold tension.
Place your object on the rubber band.
Pull back the rubber band to stretch it, and release to launch the object.
Measure how far the object travels.
Experiment with different rubber band thicknesses, lengths, and pull distances.

config.materials:

config.learn: Longer pendulum strings take more time to complete one swing (period). The experiment demonstrates how gravity and length affect oscillatory motion.

steps: Tie the weight to one end of the string.
Attach the other end of the string to a hook or tape it to a sturdy table edge.
Pull the pendulum to the side so the string is at a slight angle.
Release the pendulum and start timing with a stopwatch.
Count 10 full swings back and forth. Record the time.
Repeat using strings of different lengths and compare results.

Insert the bicycle pump needle through the cork to pressurize the bottle.
Place the bottle upside down on a flat, open surface outdoors.
Pump air slowly into the bottle until the cork pops and the bottle launches.
Measure flight distance or height. Experiment with different water levels.

Connect the free ends to the positive and negative terminals of the AA battery.
Hold the nail near paper clips and observe how it attracts them.
Experiment by changing the number of wire coils or using a larger battery.

Pour solution into the bag and mix gently.
Filter through a coffee filter into a cup.
Slowly pour cold alcohol along the side of the cup to form a separate layer.
Observe white, stringy DNA forming and spool it with a toothpick.

Observe that oil floats on top and does not mix with water.
Shake the glass gently to mix temporarily, then watch separation occur.

Add lemon juice, vinegar, or baking soda to each cup.

Rub the balloon on a wool sweater or your hair for about 20 seconds to build up charge.
Turn on the tap so a thin, steady stream of water flows into the sink.
Slowly bring the charged side of the balloon close to the stream without touching it.

Look at the pencil from the side, level with the water surface.

config.materials:

Bar magnet or refrigerator magnet
Small piece of cork or foam
Shallow bowl of water

config.learn: Stroking the needle aligns its atoms so it becomes a weak magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field. This experiment demonstrates magnetism and how a compass uses Earth's field to find direction.

steps: Stroke the needle in one direction along one end of the magnet about 30 times, lifting the magnet away between each stroke.
Cut a thin slice of cork or a small piece of foam about 1 cm wide.
Lay the magnetized needle flat on top of the cork.
Float the cork gently in the center of a bowl of water.
Let it settle and watch the needle slowly turn to point north-south.
Compare the direction with a real compass, then spin the cork and confirm it returns to the same alignment.

Release a marble from the top without pushing it and watch it roll through the track.
Measure how far the marble travels past the end of the track.

config.learn: Sound waves make the stretched surface vibrate, and the salt collects at the still points between vibrations. This experiment demonstrates standing waves and how frequency shapes vibration patterns.

steps: Stretch plastic wrap or a piece of cut balloon tightly over the open top of the can and hold it with a rubber band, making a flat drum-like surface.
Sprinkle about a teaspoon of salt evenly across the stretched surface.
Place a speaker or phone close to the surface, facing it, playing a steady low tone.
Slowly raise the pitch of the tone and watch the salt jump and gather into patterns.

config.learn: Heating turns the water to steam that pushes out air, and cooling condenses the steam so outside air pressure crushes the can. This experiment demonstrates air pressure and how gases expand and contract with temperature.

steps: Ask an adult to help, as this experiment uses heat and steam that can burn. An adult should supervise every step.

Prepare a large bowl of ice water next to the stove.
Using tongs, quickly lift the can and flip it upside down into the ice water so the opening goes under the surface.
Watch the can crush itself almost instantly, then discuss what happened.

Stand one celery stalk in each cup of colored water.
Leave the cups in a bright spot and check every few hours for a full day.

config.materials:

3 sealable plastic bags
Water spray or dropper
Labels and marker

config.learn: Mold grows fastest where there is moisture and warmth, showing what microorganisms need to thrive. This experiment demonstrates decomposition and how environmental conditions control microbial growth.

steps: Label three bags: dry, damp, and damp-dark.
Place one dry bread slice in the first bag and seal it.
Lightly spray or sprinkle a few drops of water on two other slices, then seal each in its own bag.
Keep the dry bag and one damp bag on a warm counter, and put the second damp bag in a dark cupboard.
Do not open the bags again, as mold spores should not be breathed in; only observe through the sealed plastic.
Check each bag daily for one to two weeks, recording when mold appears and how much grows in each condition, then throw the sealed bags away without opening them.

config.materials:

config.learn: Pulling the diaphragm down lowers the pressure inside so air rushes in to fill the lung. This experiment demonstrates how breathing works and how air pressure drives inhalation and exhalation.

steps: Ask an adult to cut off the bottom of a plastic bottle.
Attach a small balloon to the end of a straw and lower it inside the bottle so the balloon hangs down and the straw sticks out the top; seal around the straw with clay.
This small balloon inside represents a lung.
Cut the neck off the large balloon and stretch the wide part tightly over the open bottom of the bottle, securing it with a rubber band. This is the diaphragm.
Gently pull the stretched bottom balloon downward and watch the lung balloon inside inflate.
Push the bottom balloon back up and watch the lung balloon deflate, then repeat to model breathing.

config.materials:

config.learn: The acid in vinegar combined with salt dissolves the dull copper oxide coating and reveals shiny metal. This experiment demonstrates acid-base chemistry and how acids react with metal oxides.

steps: Pour about 50 ml of vinegar into a small bowl and stir in one teaspoon of salt until it dissolves.
Set aside one dirty penny so you can compare it later.
Dip another penny halfway into the vinegar-salt mixture and hold it for about 20 seconds.
Lift it out and compare the dipped half with the untouched half.
Drop several more pennies fully into the mixture and wait 5 minutes.
Rinse the pennies with water, dry them on a paper towel, and compare their shine to the untreated penny.

config.materials:

Water (~120 ml)

Bowl and spoon
config.learn: The contact lens solution links the glue molecules into long chains that trap the liquid, forming a stretchy polymer. This experiment demonstrates polymers and how cross-linking changes a material from liquid to gel.

steps: Pour about 120 ml of white glue into a bowl.
Stir in about 120 ml of water and a few drops of food coloring if you want.
Mix in half a teaspoon of baking soda until fully combined.
Add contact lens solution one tablespoon at a time, stirring after each addition.
Keep stirring until the mixture pulls away from the bowl and becomes stretchy.
Knead the slime with your hands for a minute, adding a tiny bit more solution if it is too sticky, then wash your hands when finished.

config.materials:
Lemon juice (~2 tbsp)
Water (few drops)
Cotton swab or thin paintbrush
White paper
Small bowl
Desk lamp with an incandescent bulb or an iron (adult use)
config.learn: Lemon juice weakens the paper and browns at a lower temperature than plain paper when heated. This experiment demonstrates oxidation and how heat can trigger a chemical color change.

steps: Mix about two tablespoons of lemon juice with a few drops of water in a small bowl.
Dip a cotton swab into the mixture and write a secret message on white paper.
Let the paper dry completely so the writing becomes invisible.

## It All Starts With Light

Have you ever looked outside to see a green apple, or a bright red cherry? Ever wondered how you see color? Well, the answer is all down to **light**!

When the sun shines down on us, it gives off white light. But this white light is actually made up of **many different colors** mixed together — just like a rainbow!

When light hits an object, some colors are absorbed and some are reflected. The colors that bounce back into your eyes are what you see!

## The Special Cells Inside Your Eyes

Your eyes contain a special layer called the **retina**. Inside the retina are tiny cells called **cones** that allow you to see color.

These cones come in three types, each sensitive to a different color of light:

- 🔴 **Red-sensitive cones**
- 🟢 **Green-sensitive cones**
- 🔵 **Blue-sensitive cones**

These three types of cones work together to let you detect millions of different colors!

## Your Brain Does the Rest

When the cones detect light, they send a message to your brain through the **optic nerve**. Your brain works like an incredibly powerful computer — it combines all the signals from your cones to figure out exactly what color you're seeing.

Your brain does all of this **so fast you don't even notice!**

## Why Color Vision Matters

This amazing ability helps us understand the world around us every single day. Color helps us:

- Recognize foods (is that fruit ripe?)
- Read signs and traffic lights
- Enjoy beautiful things like sunsets, rainbows, and the aurora borealis

Next time you admire a colorful flower or a stunning sunset, remember the incredible teamwork happening between your eyes and your brain!
config.realWorld: People who are colorblind have cones that work differently, making it hard to tell certain colors apart — most commonly red and green. Knowing this, designers make sure important signs and signals aren't based on color alone.
config.funFact: Mantis shrimp have 16 types of color receptors compared to our 3 — making them one of the most color-sensitive creatures on Earth!

## A Marvel of Engineering

Have you ever looked up at the sky to see the massive hunk of metal that is an airplane flying? Ever wondered how such a large and heavy machine can stay up in the air for hours at insane speeds?

Airplanes may look heavy, but they're designed very carefully to be able to fly. It took many scientists, pilots, and years of research to make modern airplanes fly safely.

## The Secret: Wings!

An airplane's most important component is its **enormous wings**. Air moves faster over the top of the wings than it does below them. This difference in speed creates a force called **lift** that pushes the airplane upward.

The massive engines on the wings create a separate force called **thrust** that pushes the plane forward.

## The 4 Forces of Flight

When flying, airplanes must balance **4 forces** at all times:

- **Thrust** — pushes the plane forward
- **Lift** — pushes the plane upward
- **Gravity** — pulls the plane back down to Earth
- **Drag** — slows the plane down

Lift and thrust work against gravity and drag. When these forces are in balance, the airplane can fly smoothly through the sky!

## Steering and Safety

On the airplane, there are special movable parts on the wings and tail that allow pilots to steer the plane left, right, up, or down.

Newer airplanes also use **computers for navigation** and to keep everyone on board safe. Because of science and engineering, airplanes can take people all around the world in a matter of hours!
config.realWorld: Every time you board a plane, you're experiencing centuries of physics and engineering at work. The same principles of lift and drag that make planes fly also apply to birds, kites, and even race cars (which use wings to push DOWN for better grip!).
config.funFact: The wings of a large airplane like a Boeing 747 can flex up to 6 feet up and down during flight — this flexibility actually makes them stronger, not weaker!

## A Place Where Nothing Escapes

Have you ever heard of a black hole? Black holes are some of the most mysterious objects in space!

A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that **nothing can escape from it — not even light**. That is why black holes look completely dark. Scientists believe black holes form when giant stars run out of energy and collapse inward.

## Why Black Holes Matter

Black holes may sound scary, but they are actually very important in our universe. They come in all sizes:

- Some black holes are only a **few miles wide**
- Others are **millions of times bigger than our Sun!**

In the center of many galaxies, including our own **Milky Way Galaxy**, there is a supermassive black hole.

## The Parts of a Black Hole

A black hole has different parts:

- **The Singularity** — The very center, where all the matter is squeezed into a tiny point.
- **The Event Horizon** — The boundary surrounding the singularity. This is sometimes called the *"point of no return."* If something crosses the event horizon, it cannot escape the black hole's gravity.

## How Scientists Study Black Holes

Even though black holes cannot be seen directly, scientists can study them by looking at how they affect nearby stars and gas.

In **2019**, scientists captured the **first ever image of a black hole** using powerful telescopes around the world — a huge milestone for science!

Black holes help scientists learn more about space, gravity, and how the universe works!
config.realWorld: The supermassive black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy is called Sagittarius A*. Even though it's 26,000 light-years away, scientists can track stars orbiting it to study its massive gravitational pull.
config.funFact: If you could somehow fall into a black hole, time would pass slower for you than for someone watching from far away — a real phenomenon called time dilation predicted by Einstein!

## Sunlight Isn't Just White

When you look up at the sky, have you ever wondered why it's blue? This interesting phenomenon is due to the air and sunlight all around us!

Sunlight may look white, but it's actually a **bunch of different colors mixed together**. Think about a rainbow — all those colors are hiding inside sunlight!

## What Happens in the Atmosphere?

When sunlight from the Sun hits Earth, it travels through tiny particles and gases in the atmosphere. These small particles, impossible to see without special tools, **scatter the light in all directions**.

Blue light gets scattered a lot more than other colors because it travels in **small, shorter waves** through the atmosphere.

## Why Blue Reaches Your Eyes

Because blue light is scattered so much, it reaches your eyes from **every single direction** — up, down, left, or right. That's why when you look up at the sky, you see blue!

Colors like red and orange don't scatter as much, which is why you don't normally see them filling the sky.

## Why Sunrises and Sunsets Are Red and Orange

You might be wondering — if red and orange don't scatter, why do we see them at sunrise and sunset?

During sunrise and sunset, the Sun is near the horizon, so sunlight has to travel a **much longer distance** through the atmosphere to reach your eyes. By the time it gets to you, most of the blue light has already scattered away — leaving the reds and oranges behind to paint the sky!
config.realWorld: Next time you watch a sunset, you're actually seeing physics in action! The gorgeous reds and oranges are what's left after all the blue light has been scattered away by the atmosphere.
config.funFact: On Mars, the sky appears pinkish-red because the dust particles in its thin atmosphere scatter red light instead of blue!

## More Than Just Rest

When you sleep, it may feel like you are doing absolutely nothing. This is very misleading! When you sleep, your brain and body are both super busy.

Sleep is a fully natural process that allows your body to recover after moving all day. When you're resting, your brain is not. It is **organizing memories, repairing your muscles, and replenishing your energy** to ensure that you are ready for the next day.

## The Stages of Sleep

Your brain isn't just doing the same task when you're asleep — it goes through **different stages**:

- Some stages are very low energy, and can make you wake up easily.
- Others are very deep, when it is hard for you to wake up.
- There's also a special stage known as **REM Sleep**, which is when you dream!

During REM Sleep, your brain is almost as active as when you are fully conscious!

## Sleep and Learning

Sleep is **essential** for your body to function and for learning and focus. After studying or learning something new, your body essentially stores the information you learned during the time you are asleep. This makes it easier to remember in the morning — making sleep very helpful before a big test or a busy day.

Without sleep, it's harder to pay attention and solve problems.

## How Much Sleep Do You Need?

Kids and teenagers need more sleep than adults. As a kid or teen, you should get **9–11 hours a day** because you are still growing!

Good sleeping habits also help your body get the rest it needs:
- Turn off screens before bed

You don't sleep just for fun — it is one of the most important functions of your body and helps you grow healthy and strong!

You know when you play video games, watch YouTube, or send messages to your friends? These things don't just magically happen — they're all thanks to a piece of technology that has defined our modern age: **the internet**.

While it may seem like wizardry, it is actually thanks to a huge connected computer system all throughout the world! It's kind of like a massive string connecting millions of devices — from smartwatches to the very device you're reading this on.

## Servers: The Brains Behind Your Search

When you search something up, you actually send a **request** using the internet to something called a **server**. This request reaches the server through cables that are sometimes even under the ocean!

A server is a powerful computer (or set of computers) that analyzes your request and, in a matter of seconds, sends the data you're looking for back to you. Servers store website data, videos, code, and all the information that comes with them.

## Packets: Breaking It All Down

The internet doesn't send everything all at once. Instead, it uses things called **packets** to break data into smaller pieces and send them separately. Each packet takes a different path through the internet and finds its way to your computer — kind of like puzzle pieces that reassemble on arrival.

These packets are the reason why you can watch videos at high quality or scroll through websites so smoothly.

## The Amazing Journey of Your Data

Next time you open your computer and visit a website, remember the incredible technological innovation that makes it possible. The internet has transformed our world, allowing us to communicate faster than ever and experience things our ancestors couldn't even dream of — like playing games online or chatting with friends across the globe.

Remember the super amazing, speedy journey your data takes every single time you go online!

## Hydropower Has BOOMED

Hydropower has boomed in the past century, so much so that it produces almost **twenty percent of the world's energy**! But how does it work? Imagine a river rushing downstream after a wild storm — the water is moving at crazy speeds. People capture the energy from the water's speed and use it to power things like our homes, schools, and even our smartphones.

## How Do We Convert Water's Speed Into Energy?

Usually, hydropower plants are built close to dams. This way, whenever energy is needed, the dam can quickly release water so the immense speed of it can convert into energy. It is converted by something called **turbines** — turbines are like massive fans, except they have many large blades. When the water rushes past, it spins the turbines extremely fast. But how does a spinning turbine turn into electricity?

## The Generator's Magic

The rapidly spinning turbines are connected to a special machine called a **generator**. The generator is how spinning turbines become electricity. It turns the *kinetic energy* of the turbine — the energy it has because of its motion — into electricity. It's similar to a bicycle: the faster you pedal, the more energy is produced. But here, it's on a much larger scale. All in all, the faster the turbine spins, the more electricity is produced.

## Why Hydropower Is Special

Hydropower is extremely special because, unlike other energy sources, **it does not go away!** You can use the same water multiple times to spin the same turbines — making it a **renewable source of energy**. It also does not create smoke or pollution.

However, hydropower must be used cautiously. Building dams can affect fish, plants, and nearby communities. When used wisely, hydropower is one of the smartest ways to use nature to power our planet and brighten our world.
config.realWorld: The next time you flip on a light switch, there's a good chance the electricity came from a hydropower plant! Major rivers across the world — like the Colorado and Columbia Rivers in the U.S. — have large dams that generate electricity for millions of homes every day.

activities.title: The Amazing Power of the Atom ⚡

config.markdown:
The word *nuclear* can sound intimidating, but it actually describes something incredibly small — **atoms**! Atoms make up everything around you, from the device you're reading this on to your very own hands and eyes. They're so tiny that you'd need a special microscope just to see them. Yet, right at the center of every atom (called the **nucleus**) sits a massive amount of untapped energy — just waiting to be unleashed. And scientists have figured out exactly how to turn that energy into electricity!

## How Does Nuclear Power Work?

Nuclear power plants create electricity without burning fossil fuels. Instead, they use a process called **nuclear fission**, which splits atoms apart to release energy in the form of heat.

This heat warms up water, turning it into steam — which is why you see those big clouds rising from nuclear power plants. That steam then spins massive machines called **turbines**, which generate electricity. That electricity flows out to power schools, homes, businesses, and yes — even your TV!

## Why Is Nuclear Energy So Special?

Unlike coal or gas, nuclear energy does **not** release CO₂ into the atmosphere. That means it doesn't contribute to air pollution or speed up climate change the way burning fossil fuels does. It's one of the most powerful and clean energy sources we have.

## The One Catch

Here's the caveat: nuclear energy does produce a dangerous byproduct called **nuclear waste**. If not handled carefully, this waste could be harmful to people and the environment. The good news? Scientists have developed safe methods to store nuclear waste so it doesn't cause damage. It's one of the most carefully managed materials on Earth.

## Small Things, Big Power

Next time you flip a light switch or turn on your TV, remember — that electricity might be coming from the inside of an atom! Nuclear energy is proof that the smallest things in existence can lead to the biggest outcomes.
config.realWorld: About 20% of the electricity in the United States comes from nuclear power plants. Countries like France generate over 70% of their electricity from nuclear energy. It's one of the largest sources of clean energy on the planet.
config.funFact: A single uranium fuel pellet — about the size of a pencil eraser — contains as much energy as 17,000 cubic feet of natural gas, 1,780 pounds of coal, or 149 gallons of oil!

activities.title: Why Is the Statue of Liberty Green?

config.markdown:
When you think of the Statue of Liberty, you most likely picture a giant green lady holding a torch high in the air, right? Did you know that Lady Liberty is not actually green by design? When France gave the United States the statue, she was actually a reddish-brown color — like a brand new penny! This is because the Statue of Liberty is made out of a metal called **copper**, which changes dramatically over time.

## What Is Oxidation?

You may be wondering why this color change happened. It's all due to a fascinating process called **oxidation**. Over many years on Liberty Island, the copper reacted with oxygen found in rain, water, the air, and even fog! As these reactions continued, the statue gradually turned a darker brown, and finally to the iconic green color we see today.

This green layer is called a **patina**, and it can take years — even decades — to form completely.

## Is the Green Color a Bad Thing?

You might be thinking that the color change is a sign of damage, but it's actually the opposite! The patina works like a protective barrier — it shields the copper underneath, stopping it from corroding or fading away. If the patina wasn't there, the Statue of Liberty would be far more damaged than it is today.

## Nature's Own Shield

It's incredible to think that nature itself has been protecting one of the most iconic symbols of freedom for over a century. Next time you see a photo of Lady Liberty, remember — that green color isn't there for style. It serves a real and important scientific purpose.

It's amazing how chemistry quietly works to preserve history right before our eyes!
config.realWorld: Oxidation and patina formation happen on copper roofs, old coins, and outdoor sculptures all over the world. The same science that turned the Statue of Liberty green protects copper pipes in buildings and is used in chemistry and engineering every day.
config.funFact: The Statue of Liberty is covered in about 80 tons of copper — roughly the same weight as 10 elephants — and it took around 20-30 years for the copper to fully turn green after it was unveiled in 1886!

activities.title: Solar Power: How We're Catching the Sun's Energy

config.markdown:
5 billion years ago, a massive ball of burning gas exploded into existence. This very ball became known as the Sun — the very thing that lights up our entire solar system! You may not think about this often, but did you know that the Sun sends more energy to Earth in just one hour than every single human uses in an entire year? And here's the wildest part: we've found a way to catch and turn this energy into usable electricity. This invention is known as solar power, and the world is changing because of it!

## How Do We "Catch" Sunlight?

It all comes down to solar panels, which are made up of tiny units called **photovoltaic cells**. I know — it's a tongue twister! But when sunlight hits these cells, it knocks tiny particles loose and creates electricity. Think of it like dominoes, but instead of dominoes, it's millions of particles hitting the cell. It sounds like something out of Star Wars, but this technology is everywhere. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope runs on solar power while floating in outer space, and some of your everyday calculators and streetlights use tiny solar cells too!

## Solar Power in the Real World

Many skeptics believe solar energy is some far-fetched futuristic concept that will never be widely used — but that's far from the truth. Take **Babcock Ranch** in Florida, for example. It's America's first fully solar-powered town. Over 700 solar panels power every single home there! Just imagine — all of your power, and all of your neighbors' power, coming straight from the sun.

And this doesn't just apply to small towns. Big companies like **Apple** and **Google** have switched most of their offices to solar power. This isn't just some far-fetched idea anymore — it's the future!

## Why Does It Matter?

One simple answer: pollution. Our old electricity comes from burning fossil fuels — coal and gas — which put harmful gases into the air and speed up climate change. Solar energy produces the same electricity, but without hurting our environment.

Countries like the US, China, and Germany are already racing to make the switch, and the pace is only picking up. This is truly historic — our world has relied on fossil fuels as the main source of energy for centuries, but we are finally transitioning to something better. You're growing up right in the middle of this shift, which is kind of a big deal. Maybe one day, it'll even be you designing the solar technology that powers the next generation!
config.realWorld: Babcock Ranch in Florida is America's first fully solar-powered town. Companies like Apple, Google, and NASA already run on solar energy. Solar panels can be found on rooftops, in space, and even on small everyday devices like calculators.
config.funFact: The Sun delivers more energy to Earth in just ONE hour than all of humanity uses in an entire year — and solar panels let us tap into that incredible power!

activities.title: How Bionic Limbs Are Changing Lives

config.markdown:
Almost 5,000 children lose their limbs every year, but some of these children are able to live completely normal lives. You may be thinking "how is someone able to live a normal life without an arm or leg?". This miracle is thanks to the invention of bionic limbs. Some may mistake bionic limbs to be the things they see in movies, with rockets coming out, like Cyborg from Teen Titans Go. The truth is that bionic arms are even better — they give people the gift of being able to move something they thought they lost. It gives people hope.

Modern day bionic limbs, like the Hero Arm, have special sensors that sense muscle movement. This means that when your brain sends a signal to your arm to move, the sensors detect this in advance and move the limb. This is life-changing technology for many people who have lost their limb. After getting an arm or leg removed, simple tasks — like holding a coffee mug, simply writing a sentence, or running around with your friends — become impossible. Imagine how hard life would be if you could not do any of these things. Things you hated, like writing essays, become something you yearn for. It's very easy to take such things for granted.

Many people believe that it is hard to remain an athlete after losing a limb, however that is far from the truth. A great example of this is Jeremy Campbell. He is a widely successful Olympic athlete who even won a gold medal in the Paralympics. He is a discus thrower who uses a prosthetic leg to succeed in his event. You may be wondering why you need legs for discus throwing, but you need a lot of advanced footwork to succeed. A prosthetic leg allows him to compete and even get a gold medal! Without this, he wouldn't even be able to think about competing at the highest level of sport.

Thanks to the introduction of prosthetic limbs, many lives have been changed for the better. People have been able to go against all odds and become whatever they want to be, and reach their full potential. Just like Jeremy Campbell, all children that have lost a limb can reach the Olympics — or simply run around with their friends like any other child.
config.realWorld: Bionic and prosthetic limbs are used by thousands of people around the world today, from Paralympic athletes to kids who just want to play with their friends. Companies like Open Bionics make the Hero Arm — a real, affordable bionic arm that kids can actually use.
config.funFact: Jeremy Campbell won a gold medal in discus throwing at the Paralympics — using a prosthetic leg! Advanced footwork is key to throwing a discus, and his prosthetic made it possible.

config.markdown:
## The Mystery of Floating Ice

Have you ever noticed that ice cubes float in your drink instead of sinking to the bottom? This might seem normal, but it's actually one of the coolest things about water! Most substances sink when they freeze, but water does the opposite. Let's explore why!

---

## What Makes Water So Special?

### The Science of Water Molecules

Water is made up of tiny particles called **molecules**. Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom (that's why we call it H₂O!).

### What Happens When Water Freezes?

When water gets cold enough to freeze (32°F or 0°C), something amazing happens:

1. **The molecules slow down** - As water cools, its molecules move slower and slower
2. **They form a special pattern** - The molecules arrange themselves into a honeycomb-like crystal structure
3. **They spread apart** - This pattern actually takes up MORE space than liquid water!

### The Result: Ice is Less Dense

Because ice takes up more space than the same amount of liquid water, it's **less dense**. And here's the rule: **less dense things float on more dense things!**

---

## Why Does This Matter?

### For Animals and Nature

- **Fish survive winter** because ice floats on top of lakes and ponds, creating an insulating layer that keeps the water below from freezing solid
- **Aquatic plants** can continue to live and make oxygen under the ice
- **The entire ecosystem** of a lake depends on this special property!

### For Our Planet

- **Icebergs float** in the ocean, with about 90% hidden underwater
- **Polar ice caps** float on the Arctic Ocean
- **Ocean currents** are affected by how ice and water interact

---

## Try This at Home!

### Experiment 1: The Floating Ice Test
**Materials:** Glass, water, ice cubes

1. Fill a glass with water
2. Gently place ice cubes in the water
3. Watch how much of the ice stays above vs. below the water line
4. Mark the water level and check it again after the ice melts - did it change?

### Experiment 2: Compare with Other Liquids
**Materials:** Cooking oil, water, ice cubes, two glasses

1. Put ice in a glass of water - it floats!
2. Put ice in a glass of cooking oil - what happens?
3. Why do you think the results are different?

---

## Key Vocabulary

- **Density:** How tightly packed molecules are in a substance
- **Molecule:** The smallest unit of a substance that still has all its properties
- **Crystal structure:** A repeating pattern of molecules
- **Insulating:** Protecting from temperature changes
config.realWorld: This property of water is essential for life! Fish, frogs, and other aquatic creatures survive frozen winters because ice forms a protective layer on top of lakes and ponds, while the water below stays liquid.
config.funFact: About 90% of an iceberg is hidden underwater - that's where the phrase 'tip of the iceberg' comes from! The Titanic hit an iceberg in 1912 because the crew couldn't see how massive it really was below the surface.

q.bank.human-body.077.explanation: The stomach and intestines break food down so your body can use it.

q.bank.human-body.078.prompt: Which organ controls your body and lets you think, move, and feel?
q.bank.human-body.078.explanation: The brain is the body's control center for thinking, moving, and sensing.

q.bank.human-body.079.prompt: Red blood cells carry which gas from your lungs to the rest of your body?
q.bank.human-body.079.explanation: Red blood cells pick up oxygen in the lungs and deliver it around the body.

q.bank.human-body.080.prompt: The nervous system sends messages using special cells called what?
q.bank.human-body.080.explanation: Neurons are nerve cells that carry signals throughout your body.

q.bank.human-body.081.prompt: Which part of the digestive system absorbs most of the nutrients from food?
q.bank.human-body.081.explanation: The small intestine takes in most of the nutrients your food provides.

q.bank.ecosystems.082.prompt: A place where an animal lives and finds food, water, and shelter is called its what?
q.bank.ecosystems.082.explanation: A habitat is the natural home where an animal gets everything it needs.

q.bank.ecosystems.083.prompt: In a food chain, what is usually the main starting source of energy?
q.bank.ecosystems.083.explanation: The sun's energy is captured by plants, which begin most food chains.

q.bank.ecosystems.084.prompt: Which of these is a living thing in an ecosystem?
q.bank.ecosystems.084.explanation: A rabbit is alive, while rocks, sunlight, and water are nonliving parts.

q.bank.ecosystems.085.prompt: Bees moving pollen from flower to flower help plants do what?
q.bank.ecosystems.085.explanation: When bees carry pollen, they help flowers make seeds and fruit.

q.bank.ecosystems.086.prompt: Animals that hunt and eat other animals for food are called what?
q.bank.ecosystems.086.explanation: Predators are animals that catch and eat other animals, called prey.

q.bank.ecosystems.087.prompt: In a food web, which living things make their own food using sunlight?
q.bank.ecosystems.087.explanation: Producers, such as green plants, make their own food using sunlight.

q.bank.ecosystems.088.prompt: What do decomposers like mushrooms and earthworms do in an ecosystem?
choices: Break down dead plants and animals
q.bank.ecosystems.088.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients by breaking down things that have died.

q.bank.ecosystems.089.prompt: If all the plants in a food chain disappeared, what would most likely happen to the plant-eaters?
choices: They would have no food and struggle to survive
q.bank.ecosystems.089.explanation: Plant-eaters depend on plants for energy, so losing plants would leave them hungry.

q.bank.ecosystems.090.prompt: What do we call all the different kinds of living things found in an area?
q.bank.ecosystems.090.explanation: Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place.

q.bank.ecosystems.091.prompt: When one type of living thing is suddenly removed, a food web can become what?
q.bank.ecosystems.091.explanation: Every living thing is connected, so removing one can throw the web out of balance.

q.bank.ecosystems.092.prompt: Two animals that both need the same limited food are said to be in what with each other?
q.bank.ecosystems.092.explanation: Competition happens when living things must share a limited resource like food.

q.bank.cells-genetics.093.prompt: What is the smallest building block that makes up all living things?
q.bank.cells-genetics.093.explanation: Cells are the tiny basic units that make up every living thing.

q.bank.cells-genetics.094.prompt: Traits like the color of your eyes are passed down from whom?
q.bank.cells-genetics.094.explanation: You inherit traits like eye color from your parents.

q.bank.cells-genetics.095.prompt: Which of these is an inherited trait you were born with?
choices: Knowing how to ride a bike
The natural color of your hair
q.bank.cells-genetics.095.explanation: Natural hair color is inherited, while the others are things you learn.

q.bank.cells-genetics.096.prompt: A baby animal usually looks most similar to its what?
q.bank.cells-genetics.096.explanation: Baby animals resemble their parents because they inherit their traits.

q.bank.cells-genetics.097.prompt: What is the control center of a cell that holds its instructions?
q.bank.cells-genetics.097.explanation: The nucleus stores the cell's instructions and directs what the cell does.

q.bank.cells-genetics.098.prompt: The instructions inside your cells that decide your traits are made of what?
q.bank.cells-genetics.098.explanation: DNA carries the coded instructions that shape your traits.

q.bank.cells-genetics.099.prompt: Which of these is a learned behavior rather than an inherited trait?
q.bank.cells-genetics.099.explanation: Reading is learned through practice, while the others are inherited traits.

q.bank.cells-genetics.100.prompt: Plant cells have a stiff outer layer that animal cells do not have, called what?
q.bank.cells-genetics.100.explanation: The cell wall gives plant cells extra support and structure.

q.bank.cells-genetics.101.prompt: Which part of the cell makes energy the cell can use, often called the powerhouse?
q.bank.cells-genetics.101.explanation: Mitochondria release energy from food so the cell can work.

q.bank.cells-genetics.102.prompt: Genes are found on tiny thread-like structures inside the nucleus called what?
q.bank.cells-genetics.102.explanation: Chromosomes are structures made of DNA that carry your genes.

q.bank.cells-genetics.103.prompt: Offspring often show a mix of traits from both parents because they receive what?
q.bank.cells-genetics.103.explanation: Each parent passes on genes, so offspring blend traits from both.

q.bank.earth-weather.104.prompt: What is falling from the sky when it rains, snows, sleets, or hails?
q.bank.earth-weather.104.explanation: Precipitation is water that falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

q.bank.earth-weather.105.prompt: Which of these do we see in the sky and is made of tiny water droplets?
q.bank.earth-weather.105.explanation: Clouds are made of many tiny water droplets floating in the air.

q.bank.earth-weather.106.prompt: What do we call the day-to-day conditions outside, like sunny, rainy, or windy?
q.bank.earth-weather.106.explanation: Weather is what the air and sky are like outside right now.

q.bank.earth-weather.107.prompt: The sun gives Earth which two important things?
q.bank.earth-weather.107.explanation: The sun provides Earth with light and heat that living things need.

q.bank.earth-weather.108.prompt: In the water cycle, what is it called when the sun heats water and it turns into a gas?
q.bank.earth-weather.108.explanation: Evaporation is when liquid water warms up and changes into water vapor.

q.bank.earth-weather.109.prompt: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
Weather is right now, while climate is the usual pattern over many years
q.bank.earth-weather.109.explanation: Weather is the short-term conditions, and climate is the long-term average pattern.

q.bank.earth-weather.110.prompt: Clouds form when water vapor in the air cools and turns back into tiny droplets during what?
q.bank.earth-weather.110.explanation: Condensation is when water vapor cools and becomes liquid droplets, forming clouds.

q.bank.earth-weather.111.prompt: Which type of cloud is puffy, white, and looks like cotton on a nice day?
q.bank.earth-weather.111.explanation: Cumulus clouds are the puffy, cotton-like clouds seen on fair days.

q.bank.earth-weather.112.prompt: Earth's seasons are mainly caused by what?
choices: The tilt of Earth's axis as it orbits the sun
The sun turning off at night
q.bank.earth-weather.112.explanation: Earth is tilted, so different parts get more direct sunlight at different times of year.

q.bank.earth-weather.113.prompt: Which layer of gases surrounds Earth and holds the air we breathe and our weather?
q.bank.earth-weather.113.explanation: The atmosphere is the blanket of gases around Earth where weather happens.

q.bank.earth-weather.114.prompt: Warm air does what compared to cool air, which helps create wind and weather?
choices: It sinks straight to the ground
It rises because it is lighter
q.bank.earth-weather.114.explanation: Warm air is lighter than cool air, so it rises and helps set air moving.

q.bank.rocks-resources.115.prompt: What natural material is made of tiny bits of broken rock and helps plants grow?
q.bank.rocks-resources.115.explanation: Soil is a mix of tiny rock pieces and other matter that plants grow in.

q.bank.rocks-resources.116.prompt: Which of these is a natural resource that comes from the Earth?
q.bank.rocks-resources.116.explanation: Water is a natural resource we get from the Earth and need to live.

q.bank.rocks-resources.117.prompt: What do we call using items again instead of throwing them away, like cans and paper?
q.bank.rocks-resources.117.explanation: Recycling turns used materials into new products and saves resources.

q.bank.rocks-resources.118.prompt: A mountain that can erupt with hot melted rock is called a what?
q.bank.rocks-resources.118.explanation: A volcano is an opening in Earth where melted rock can erupt to the surface.

q.bank.rocks-resources.119.prompt: Rocks that form from cooled, hardened melted rock are called what type?
q.bank.rocks-resources.119.explanation: Igneous rocks form when melted rock cools and hardens.

q.bank.rocks-resources.120.prompt: The slow wearing away of rock and soil by wind and water is called what?
q.bank.rocks-resources.120.explanation: Erosion is when wind or water slowly carries away bits of rock and soil.

q.bank.rocks-resources.121.prompt: Which of these energy sources is renewable, meaning it will not run out?
q.bank.rocks-resources.121.explanation: Sunlight is renewable because the sun keeps providing energy every day.

q.bank.rocks-resources.122.prompt: Preserved remains or prints of ancient living things found in rock are called what?
q.bank.rocks-resources.122.explanation: Fossils are traces of ancient life saved in rock over a very long time.

q.bank.rocks-resources.123.prompt: Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sediment press together over time; which rock is sedimentary?
q.bank.rocks-resources.123.explanation: Sandstone forms from layers of sand pressed together, making it sedimentary.

q.bank.rocks-resources.124.prompt: Earthquakes happen when large pieces of Earth's crust, called plates, do what?
choices: Suddenly move or slip past each other
q.bank.rocks-resources.124.explanation: Earthquakes are the shaking caused when Earth's plates suddenly shift.

q.bank.rocks-resources.125.prompt: Which of these is a nonrenewable resource that can run out if we use too much?
q.bank.rocks-resources.125.explanation: Coal is nonrenewable because it takes millions of years to form and cannot be quickly replaced.

q.bank.space-astronomy.126.prompt: Which object in the sky gives Earth most of its light and heat during the day?
q.bank.space-astronomy.126.explanation: The Sun is our closest star, and its energy gives us the light and warmth we feel every day.

q.bank.space-astronomy.127.prompt: What do we call the round object that orbits Earth and seems to change shape in the sky each month?
q.bank.space-astronomy.127.explanation: The Moon orbits Earth, and we see it appear to change shape as it goes through its phases.

q.bank.space-astronomy.128.prompt: How many planets are in our solar system?
q.bank.space-astronomy.128.explanation: Our solar system has eight planets, from Mercury closest to the Sun out to Neptune.

q.bank.space-astronomy.129.prompt: What makes Earth have daytime and nighttime?
choices: The Sun turns off at night
q.bank.space-astronomy.129.explanation: Earth spins once about every 24 hours, so the side facing the Sun has day while the other side has night.

q.bank.space-astronomy.130.prompt: What causes the different phases of the Moon that we see from Earth?
choices: Earth's shadow always covers part of it
We see different amounts of its sunlit half
q.bank.space-astronomy.130.explanation: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different portions of its sunlit half, which creates the phases.

q.bank.space-astronomy.131.prompt: Which planet is often called the 'Red Planet'?
q.bank.space-astronomy.131.explanation: Mars looks reddish because its surface is covered with iron-rich dust that acts a bit like rust.

q.bank.space-astronomy.132.prompt: Which force keeps the planets moving in their orbits around the Sun?
q.bank.space-astronomy.132.explanation: The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them traveling along their orbits.

q.bank.space-astronomy.133.prompt: What is the main job of a telescope?
choices: To make far-away objects look larger and clearer
To send radio signals to space
q.bank.space-astronomy.133.explanation: A telescope gathers light so distant objects like stars and planets look bigger and brighter to us.

q.bank.space-astronomy.134.prompt: What is the main reason Earth has different seasons?
choices: Earth's changing distance from the Sun
q.bank.space-astronomy.134.explanation: Earth is tilted on its axis, so different parts of the planet get more direct sunlight at different times of the year.

q.bank.space-astronomy.135.prompt: What is the Sun mostly made of?
q.bank.space-astronomy.135.explanation: The Sun is a giant ball of hot gas made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

choices: How long a year lasts on a planet
The distance light travels in one year
q.bank.space-astronomy.136.explanation: A light-year is a distance equal to how far light travels in one year, which is a very long way.

q.bank.space-astronomy.137.prompt: Why does an astronaut appear to float inside a spaceship that is orbiting Earth?
choices: There is no gravity at all in space
They are constantly falling around Earth while moving forward
Their suits are filled with helium
q.bank.space-astronomy.137.explanation: The spaceship and astronaut both fall toward Earth while speeding forward, so they keep falling around it and feel weightless.

q.bank.engineering-design.138.prompt: What is usually the first step engineers take when solving a problem?
choices: Build the final product right away
Understand and clearly define the problem
q.bank.engineering-design.138.explanation: Engineers start by understanding the problem so they know exactly what their design needs to solve.

choices: A finished product ready for sale
A drawing that can never change
An early test version of a design
q.bank.engineering-design.139.explanation: A prototype is an early model engineers build to test their ideas before making the final version.

q.bank.engineering-design.140.prompt: Which shape is often used in bridges and towers because it is very strong?
q.bank.engineering-design.140.explanation: Triangles hold their shape well under pressure, which makes structures built with them very sturdy.

q.bank.engineering-design.141.prompt: What do we call a person who designs and builds things to solve problems?
q.bank.engineering-design.141.explanation: Engineers use science and math to design and build solutions to everyday problems.

q.bank.engineering-design.142.prompt: In the engineering design process, what should you do after testing a prototype?
choices: Use what you learned to improve the design
q.bank.engineering-design.142.explanation: Testing shows what works and what does not, so engineers use that information to make the design better.

q.bank.engineering-design.143.prompt: Why do engineers test their designs many times?
choices: Because a rule says they must
To find and fix problems before the final build
q.bank.engineering-design.143.explanation: Repeated testing helps engineers catch problems early and improve the design before it is finished.

q.bank.engineering-design.144.prompt: Which material would an engineer most likely choose to build a bridge that must hold heavy trucks?
q.bank.engineering-design.144.explanation: Steel is very strong and can support heavy loads, which makes it a good choice for big bridges.

choices: A machine that can be programmed to do tasks
q.bank.engineering-design.145.explanation: A robot is a machine that follows programmed instructions to carry out tasks, sometimes on its own.

q.bank.engineering-design.146.prompt: Why do many bridges and tall buildings include small gaps called expansion joints?
choices: To let the materials expand and shrink with temperature changes
q.bank.engineering-design.146.explanation: Materials grow slightly when hot and shrink when cold, and the gaps give them room to move without cracking.

q.bank.engineering-design.147.prompt: What does it mean to 'iterate' during the engineering design process?
choices: To copy someone else's finished work
To repeat and improve a design based on test results
To finish the design in only one try
q.bank.engineering-design.147.explanation: Iterating means going through the design steps again to make each version better than the last.

q.bank.engineering-design.148.prompt: Which design would most likely stay stable in strong wind?
choices: A tall, narrow tower with a tiny base
A wide base that gets narrower toward the top
q.bank.engineering-design.148.explanation: A wide, low base spreads out the weight and helps keep a structure from tipping over.

q.bank.engineering-design.149.prompt: Why do engineers often build models or run computer simulations before making a real product?
choices: Because real materials do not exist
To test ideas safely and cheaply before spending on the real thing
So they never have to test at all
q.bank.engineering-design.149.explanation: Models and simulations let engineers try out ideas and spot problems without the cost or risk of building the real thing first.

q.bank.technology-computers.150.prompt: A computer mouse is an example of what kind of device?
q.bank.technology-computers.150.explanation: A mouse sends information into the computer when you move and click it, so it is an input device.

q.bank.technology-computers.151.prompt: Which device is an output that shows you pictures and words?
q.bank.technology-computers.151.explanation: A monitor displays the computer's output so you can see images, text, and videos.

q.bank.technology-computers.152.prompt: Which of these is a good rule for staying safe online?
choices: Share your home address with strangers
Click on every pop-up you see
Post your school's name to new online friends
q.bank.technology-computers.152.explanation: Keeping passwords private helps protect your accounts and personal information from people who should not have them.

q.bank.technology-computers.153.prompt: What do we call a clear set of step-by-step instructions for completing a task?
q.bank.technology-computers.153.explanation: An algorithm is a list of ordered steps that tells a computer or person exactly how to do something.

q.bank.technology-computers.154.prompt: In coding, what does a 'loop' do?
choices: Changes the screen color one time
q.bank.technology-computers.154.explanation: A loop lets a program run the same instructions over and over without writing them out each time.

q.bank.technology-computers.155.prompt: Why does the order of steps matter in a computer program?
choices: It does not matter at all
Computers follow the steps in sequence, so the order changes the result
q.bank.technology-computers.155.explanation: Computers carry out instructions in the exact order given, so changing the order can change what happens.

choices: A single computer in one building
A huge network that connects computers around the world
A program you buy only once
q.bank.technology-computers.156.explanation: The internet is a giant network linking millions of computers so they can share information worldwide.

q.bank.technology-computers.157.prompt: What is a sensor on a device used for?
choices: To detect information like light, heat, or motion
q.bank.technology-computers.157.explanation: A sensor detects things in the world, such as light or movement, and turns them into signals the device can use.

q.bank.technology-computers.158.prompt: What does a computer's CPU mainly do?
choices: Carries out instructions and does calculations
q.bank.technology-computers.158.explanation: The CPU is like the computer's brain, following instructions and doing the calculations that make programs work.

q.bank.technology-computers.159.prompt: Why is it smart to use a strong, unique password for important accounts?
choices: So it is easier to share
To make it harder for others to guess and get into your account
q.bank.technology-computers.159.explanation: A strong, unique password is hard to guess, which helps keep your accounts and information secure.

q.bank.technology-computers.160.prompt: What is the difference between hardware and software?
choices: Hardware is the physical parts, and software is the programs and instructions
They are exactly the same thing
Hardware is on the internet and software is not
Software is the physical parts you can touch
q.bank.technology-computers.160.explanation: Hardware is the equipment you can touch, while software is the coded programs that tell the hardware what to do.

choices: Adding more bugs to a program
Finding and fixing errors in the code
q.bank.technology-computers.161.explanation: Debugging is the process of finding mistakes in code and fixing them so the program works correctly.

q.bank.science-all-stars.162.prompt: Which scientist is famous for describing gravity and the laws of motion?
q.bank.science-all-stars.162.explanation: Isaac Newton described how gravity pulls objects together and wrote the famous laws of motion.

q.bank.science-all-stars.163.prompt: Jane Goodall is best known for studying which animals in the wild?
q.bank.science-all-stars.163.explanation: Jane Goodall spent many years observing wild chimpanzees and learning about their behavior.

q.bank.science-all-stars.164.prompt: Thomas Edison helped develop a practical version of which everyday invention?
q.bank.science-all-stars.164.explanation: Edison and his team developed a long-lasting electric light bulb that people could use in their homes.

q.bank.science-all-stars.165.prompt: Which scientist is famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
q.bank.science-all-stars.165.explanation: Charles Darwin explained how living things change over many generations through natural selection.

q.bank.science-all-stars.166.prompt: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes for her groundbreaking research on what?
q.bank.science-all-stars.166.explanation: Marie Curie studied radioactivity and even discovered new elements, earning two Nobel Prizes.

q.bank.science-all-stars.167.prompt: Katherine Johnson was a mathematician who helped NASA do what?
choices: Calculate the flight paths for spaceflights
q.bank.science-all-stars.167.explanation: Katherine Johnson's careful calculations helped guide astronauts safely on their journeys to space and back.

q.bank.science-all-stars.168.prompt: George Washington Carver is well known for his research on which crop and its many uses?
q.bank.science-all-stars.168.explanation: Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts and taught farmers ways to keep their soil healthy.

q.bank.science-all-stars.169.prompt: Nikola Tesla made important contributions to which kind of electricity system?
q.bank.science-all-stars.169.explanation: Tesla helped develop the alternating current system that carries electricity to homes and buildings today.

q.bank.science-all-stars.170.prompt: Albert Einstein is most famous for developing which idea?
q.bank.science-all-stars.170.explanation: Einstein's theory of relativity changed how scientists understand space, time, and gravity.

q.bank.science-all-stars.171.prompt: Benjamin Franklin's famous experiments helped show that lightning is a form of what?
q.bank.science-all-stars.171.explanation: Franklin's experiments demonstrated that lightning is a powerful natural form of electricity.

q.bank.science-all-stars.172.prompt: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images were key to discovering the structure of which molecule?
q.bank.science-all-stars.172.explanation: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs helped reveal that DNA has a twisted, double-helix shape.

q.bank.science-all-stars.173.prompt: Galileo Galilei improved the telescope and used it to observe what?
q.bank.science-all-stars.173.explanation: Galileo used his improved telescope to discover four moons orbiting the planet Jupiter.

q.bank.measurement-method.174.prompt: Which tool would you use to measure how long a pencil is?
q.bank.measurement-method.174.explanation: A ruler is marked with units of length, making it the right tool for measuring how long something is.

q.bank.measurement-method.175.prompt: Which tool is used to measure temperature?
q.bank.measurement-method.175.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is.

q.bank.measurement-method.176.prompt: In the metric system, which unit is used to measure length?
q.bank.measurement-method.176.explanation: The meter is the basic metric unit for measuring length or distance.

q.bank.measurement-method.177.prompt: What is one of the first things scientists do to start learning about something?
q.bank.measurement-method.177.explanation: Careful observations help scientists gather information and ask good questions about what they notice.

choices: The final result of an experiment
A testable guess or prediction made before an experiment
q.bank.measurement-method.178.explanation: A hypothesis is an educated guess that a scientist can test with an experiment.

q.bank.measurement-method.179.prompt: Which tool would you use to measure the volume of a liquid?
q.bank.measurement-method.179.explanation: A graduated cylinder has marked lines that show how much liquid it holds.

q.bank.measurement-method.180.prompt: To keep an experiment fair, what should you do with the variables?
choices: Change only one thing and keep the others the same
Change the results to fit your guess
q.bank.measurement-method.180.explanation: Changing just one variable at a time lets you know that it caused any difference you see.

q.bank.measurement-method.181.prompt: What is the difference between an observation and an inference?
choices: They are exactly the same thing
An inference uses only your eyes
An observation is something you sense directly, while an inference is a conclusion you reason out
An observation is always a guess
q.bank.measurement-method.181.explanation: You make an observation using your senses, and you make an inference by using those observations to reach a conclusion.

q.bank.measurement-method.182.prompt: In a fair test, what is the variable you change on purpose called?
q.bank.measurement-method.182.explanation: The independent variable is the one thing the experimenter deliberately changes to see its effect.

q.bank.measurement-method.183.prompt: What is the main purpose of a control group in an experiment?
choices: To make the experiment take longer
To provide a comparison that stays unchanged
q.bank.measurement-method.183.explanation: A control group is left unchanged so scientists can compare it to the group they are testing.

q.bank.measurement-method.184.prompt: Which metric unit would best measure the mass of an apple?
q.bank.measurement-method.184.explanation: Mass is measured in grams and kilograms, so grams work well for something as light as an apple.

q.bank.measurement-method.185.prompt: What is a conclusion in the scientific method?
choices: A guess made before the experiment
A statement of what the results show
A list of the tools you used
q.bank.measurement-method.185.explanation: A conclusion sums up what the experiment's results tell you and whether they support your hypothesis.

q.quiz.physics.00.prompt: Why does a balloon-powered car move forward when air rushes out the back?
choices: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Wind from the room pushes it
q.quiz.physics.00.explanation: Newton's Third Law! Air rushing backward pushes the car forward with equal force.

q.quiz.physics.01.prompt: What happens to a pendulum's swing time when you make the string longer?
q.quiz.physics.01.explanation: Longer pendulums have a longer period — each swing takes more time. That's how grandfather clocks keep time!

q.quiz.physics.02.prompt: A stretched rubber band stores what kind of energy?
q.quiz.physics.02.explanation: Stretching stores elastic potential energy, which turns into kinetic (motion) energy when released.

q.quiz.physics.03.prompt: What force pulls a water bottle rocket back down to the ground?
q.quiz.physics.03.explanation: Gravity pulls everything on Earth downward at 9.8 m/s² — rockets included!

q.quiz.physics.04.prompt: Wrapping more wire coils around a nail makes an electromagnet...
q.quiz.physics.04.explanation: More coils = more magnetic field. Current flowing through each loop adds to the magnet's strength.

q.quiz.physics.05.prompt: At what angle does a launched ball travel the farthest (with no air resistance)?
q.quiz.physics.05.explanation: 45° is the perfect balance between going up and going forward — try it in the Physics Playground!

q.quiz.physics.06.prompt: In a Rube Goldberg machine, what passes from one step to the next?
q.quiz.physics.06.explanation: Each step transfers energy to the next — a rolling marble's motion energy knocks over dominoes, and so on.

q.quiz.physics.07.prompt: Why does a heavier balloon car move slower than a lighter one with the same balloon?
choices: More mass needs more force to accelerate
q.quiz.physics.07.explanation: Newton's Second Law: F = ma. With the same force, more mass means less acceleration.

q.quiz.physics.08.prompt: Sound travels as a wave of...
q.quiz.physics.08.explanation: Sound is vibrating molecules bumping into their neighbors — that's why it can't travel through empty space.

q.quiz.physics.09.prompt: Why does a pencil look bent when half of it is underwater?
choices: Light changes speed and direction entering water
Your eyes are tricked by color
q.quiz.physics.09.explanation: Light refracts — it changes direction when it moves between air and water because it travels at different speeds in each.

q.quiz.physics.10.prompt: Rubbing a balloon on your hair charges it with...
q.quiz.physics.10.explanation: Electrons rub off your hair onto the balloon, giving it a negative static charge that can attract water and paper.

q.quiz.physics.11.prompt: A compass needle points north because...
choices: The needle is heavier on one end
Earth itself is a giant magnet
q.quiz.physics.11.explanation: Earth's molten iron core creates a magnetic field, and a magnetized needle aligns itself with it.

q.quiz.chemistry.00.prompt: What gas makes the baking soda volcano erupt?
q.quiz.chemistry.00.explanation: Baking soda (a base) reacts with vinegar (an acid) to make carbon dioxide gas — all those bubbles push the 'lava' out!

q.quiz.chemistry.01.prompt: Why does oil float on top of water?
choices: Oil is less dense than water
q.quiz.chemistry.01.explanation: Density is mass per volume. Oil is less dense than water, so it floats — they don't mix because oil is hydrophobic.

q.quiz.chemistry.02.prompt: Red cabbage juice turns RED when you add something...
q.quiz.chemistry.02.explanation: Cabbage juice is a pH indicator: acids turn it red/pink, bases turn it green/blue.

q.quiz.chemistry.03.prompt: In the milk experiment, what does dish soap do to make the colors swirl?
q.quiz.chemistry.03.explanation: Soap molecules break the milk's surface tension and chase fat molecules, dragging the food coloring around!

q.quiz.chemistry.04.prompt: Crystals grow from a solution when it becomes...
q.quiz.chemistry.04.explanation: A supersaturated solution holds more dissolved material than it can keep — the extra comes out as beautiful crystals.

q.quiz.chemistry.05.prompt: Electrolysis uses electricity to split water into which two gases?
q.quiz.chemistry.05.explanation: Water is H₂O — electricity breaks it into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂) bubbles at the two pencils.

choices: A change that makes new substances
q.quiz.chemistry.06.explanation: In a chemical reaction, substances change into NEW substances — like vinegar + baking soda making gas that wasn't there before.

q.quiz.chemistry.07.prompt: Which of these is an acid?
q.quiz.chemistry.07.explanation: Lemon juice contains citric acid — that's why it tastes sour and turns cabbage juice red.

q.quiz.chemistry.08.prompt: Why does lemon juice writing turn brown when heated?
choices: The juice oxidizes and darkens before the paper does
q.quiz.chemistry.08.explanation: The acidic juice weakens the paper fibers, so that spot browns (oxidizes) at a lower temperature — revealing the secret message.

q.quiz.chemistry.09.prompt: Slime is stretchy because glue molecules link into long chains called...
q.quiz.chemistry.09.explanation: An activator links glue's long molecules together into a tangled polymer network — stretchy like a net, not a liquid or solid.

q.quiz.chemistry.10.prompt: Why does vinegar clean a dirty penny?
choices: Its acid dissolves the copper oxide layer
q.quiz.chemistry.10.explanation: The dull coating is copper oxide. A weak acid dissolves it, exposing the shiny copper underneath.

q.quiz.chemistry.11.prompt: In a mixture of salt fully stirred into water, the salt is called the...
q.quiz.chemistry.11.explanation: The substance that dissolves is the solute; the water doing the dissolving is the solvent; together they make a solution.

q.quiz.biology.00.prompt: Why do plant stems grow toward light?
q.quiz.biology.00.explanation: Phototropism means 'turning toward light' — plants grow toward their energy source to power photosynthesis.

q.quiz.biology.01.prompt: What gas does yeast produce that inflates the balloon?
q.quiz.biology.01.explanation: Yeast eats sugar and releases carbon dioxide through fermentation — the same reason bread rises!

q.quiz.biology.02.prompt: What are the lines you see in a leaf rubbing?
choices: Veins that carry water and nutrients
q.quiz.biology.02.explanation: Leaf veins are like tiny highways carrying water, minerals, and food throughout the leaf.

q.quiz.biology.03.prompt: Why is DNA from mashed strawberries visible as white strings?
choices: DNA clumps together in cold alcohol
q.quiz.biology.03.explanation: DNA doesn't dissolve in cold alcohol, so it clumps into visible white strands you can spool on a toothpick!

choices: They make tunnels that let in air and water
q.quiz.biology.04.explanation: Worm tunnels aerate the soil and their castings add nutrients — gardeners love them!

q.quiz.biology.05.prompt: What do you need to see a plant cell's structure?
q.quiz.biology.05.explanation: Cells are far too small for our eyes — microscopes magnify them hundreds of times so we can see nuclei and cell walls.

q.quiz.biology.06.prompt: What does a seed need to germinate (start growing)?
q.quiz.biology.06.explanation: Seeds wake up with moisture, the right temperature, and oxygen — light matters more after the sprout appears.

q.quiz.biology.07.prompt: Fermentation is when microorganisms like yeast...
choices: Convert sugar into energy and gas
q.quiz.biology.07.explanation: Yeast metabolizes sugar for energy and releases CO₂ — used for thousands of years to make bread and more.

q.quiz.biology.08.prompt: Colored water climbs up a celery stalk because of...
q.quiz.biology.08.explanation: Narrow tubes called xylem pull water upward through capillary action — the same way plants drink from their roots.

q.quiz.biology.09.prompt: The ridges that make your fingerprints are unique to...
q.quiz.biology.09.explanation: No two people, not even identical twins, have the same fingerprints — they form randomly before birth.

q.quiz.biology.10.prompt: Mold grows fastest on bread that is...
q.quiz.biology.10.explanation: Mold is a fungus that thrives in warm, moist conditions — which is why bread lasts longer in the fridge.

q.quiz.biology.11.prompt: When you breathe in, your lungs fill because your diaphragm...
choices: Pulls down to make more space
q.quiz.biology.11.explanation: The diaphragm flattens downward, lowering air pressure in your chest so air rushes in — exactly like the balloon lung model.

q.quiz.engineering.00.explanation: Triangles can't be squished out of shape without changing their side lengths — that's why you see them in real bridges everywhere!

q.quiz.engineering.01.prompt: What does a catapult store before launch?
q.quiz.engineering.01.explanation: Pulling back the spoon stretches the rubber bands, storing elastic energy that becomes motion when released.

q.quiz.engineering.02.prompt: In a water filter, what is each layer's job?
q.quiz.engineering.02.explanation: Gravel catches big bits, sand catches smaller ones, and charcoal grabs tiny particles and chemicals.

q.quiz.engineering.03.prompt: An LED only lights up when the circuit is...
q.quiz.engineering.03.explanation: Electricity needs a complete path from the battery, through the LED, and back — any gap stops the flow.

q.quiz.engineering.04.prompt: What makes a balloon rocket zoom along the string?
q.quiz.engineering.04.explanation: Air rushing out the back pushes the balloon forward — thrust, just like a real rocket engine!

q.quiz.engineering.05.prompt: What should an engineer do when their design fails?
choices: Study why it failed and improve the design
q.quiz.engineering.05.explanation: Failure is data! Engineers test, learn what broke and why, redesign, and test again. That's the engineering design process.

q.quiz.engineering.06.prompt: Twisting the rubber band in a paper helicopter stores energy that becomes...
q.quiz.engineering.06.explanation: The twisted band unwinds and spins the rotors — elastic energy becomes rotational kinetic energy, creating lift!

q.quiz.engineering.07.prompt: Why do engineers test bridges with weights until they break?
choices: To find the weakest point and make it stronger
q.quiz.engineering.07.explanation: Load testing reveals exactly where a structure fails first, so the next version can be reinforced there.

q.quiz.engineering.08.prompt: A spaghetti-and-marshmallow tower stands tallest when its base is...
q.quiz.engineering.08.explanation: A wide base lowers the center of gravity and triangles resist bending — the two secrets of stable towers.

q.quiz.engineering.09.prompt: A pulley makes lifting easier by...
choices: Changing the direction of your pull and sharing the load
q.quiz.engineering.09.explanation: A pulley lets you pull down (easier) to lift up, and multiple pulleys share the weight so each pull feels lighter.

q.quiz.engineering.10.prompt: The best egg-drop lander protects the egg by...
choices: Slowing the fall and cushioning the impact
q.quiz.engineering.10.explanation: Parachutes slow the fall and soft padding spreads the impact force over more time, so the egg survives the landing.

q.quiz.engineering.11.prompt: A cam in a machine is a shaped wheel that turns rotation into...
q.quiz.engineering.11.explanation: As a cam spins, its bumpy edge pushes a follower up and down — the trick behind automaton toys and engine valves.
